Three Taverns
THREE TAV-uhrnz
proper noun (place)
A translation of the Latin Tres Tabernae, "Three Taverns," a halting-place on the Appian Way about thirty miles south of Rome.

Biblical Definition

Three Taverns was a stopping-place on the Appian Way, about thirty miles south of Rome and nearer the city than Appii Forum, where a second company of Roman believers came to meet Paul on his journey to the capital. "They came to meet us as far as Appii forum, and The three taverns: whom when Paul saw, he thanked God, and took courage" (Acts 28:15). Two groups, it seems, had set out from Rome to welcome the apostle: one reaching the farther town, another waiting at the nearer halt. Both bore the same love, and the doubled welcome doubled the encouragement. Three Taverns shares with Appii Forum the witness to the refreshing power of Christian fellowship, but it adds its own note: the eagerness of the brethren, who could not all wait at the city but pressed out along the road to be the first to greet the man whose epistle to the Romans had so fed their souls. Here the great letter and its writer met. The church that had received the most weighty doctrinal epistle in the New Testament now received its author in person — a prisoner, footsore, in chains — and honored him with the only gift they could give: themselves, come out to meet him. Three Taverns marks the meeting of truth and love, of the apostle and the people his words had shaped.

Webster 1828 Definition

A halt on the Appian Way thirty miles south of Rome (Acts 28:15) where a second company of Roman believers met Paul; with Appii Forum, the doubled welcome that turned the chained apostle's heart to thanksgiving and courage.

THREE TAVERNS, noun phrase. Latin Tres Tabernae; a halt on the Appian Way about thirty miles south of Rome.

Nearer the city than Appii Forum.

Where a second company of Roman brethren met Paul (Acts 28:15).

The doubled welcome that doubled the apostle's encouragement.

The meeting of the author of Romans with the church his epistle had fed.

Key Scripture

Acts 28:15 — "And from thence, when the brethren heard of us, they came to meet us as far as Appii forum, and The three taverns: whom when Paul saw, he thanked God, and took courage."

Rom 1:7 — "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ."

Rom 15:24 — "Whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you: for I trust to see you in my journey, and to be brought on my way thitherward by you, if first I be somewhat filled with your company."

3 John 1:14 — "But I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face. Peace be to thee. Our friends salute thee. Greet the friends by name."

Modern Corruption

Three Taverns needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the eagerness of Christian love, which presses out to meet the suffering saint, and the union of sound doctrine with warm affection.

expand to see more

Doctrine-versus-love misreading. Some imagine that a church devoted to weighty doctrine must be cold, and a warm church must be shallow. Three Taverns refutes the caricature: the very believers who had received the epistle to the Romans, the deepest doctrinal letter in the New Testament, were the ones who hurried down the road in love to meet its author. The dictionary holds that truth and love are not rivals but companions; the soundest doctrine, rightly received, produces the warmest affection.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the eagerness of love. The brethren did not wait passively but pressed out, some to the nearer halt and some to the farther, to be first to greet the prisoner. Such forward, seeking love — that will not wait to be sought but goes out to find and honor the servant of God — is the mark of a church shaped by the gospel it has believed.
